newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE-Residents fear as mobsters fight in Naples streets.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Residents fear as mobsters fight in Naples streets.

text.p: Luigi Di Pietro points to a car bumper sticker displaying the words "Welcome to the combat zone," as he weaves his taxi through the cluttered traffic of this sloping southern port city.
"That's not far from the truth," he sighed.
Di Pietro has been twice held up at gun point in the last three years by local gangsters who then stole his car.
"We're all at risk here. Violence is increasing. People are afraid. They're buying arms. Streets are empty after 9 p.m. The city is boiling over."
This week, the Italian government announced it would send a military force to Naples to help counter a wave of mob violence that has swept the region since the start of the year.

More than 80 people have been killed and dozens injured in the last six months as warring clans of the Camorra, the Naples Mafia, have fought bloody battles for supremacy in the bustling streets of the city.

"The Camorra is spreading out and taking up an attitude of such fearlessness that it feels it can settle accounts in broad daylight, without giving a thought to who is around," Naples chief prosecutor Agostino Cordova told reporters.
A LOOSE NETWORK OF BATTLING CLANS
Some 80 Camorra clans with several thousand affiliates operate in and around Naples, said anti-mob prosecutor Luigi Bobbio from the courthouse in Naples' industrial district.
Unlike the Sicilian Mafia, which has a rigid hierarchical structure with "bosses" who impose order and respect, the Camorra is loose-knit and diffuse, he said.
Prosecutors have identified three main Camorra families in the Naples area, but their control over the clans is limited.
"It's a very fragmented, confused reality. There is very little order and no respect among the clans, so if one group steps into the territory of another, war breaks out," he says.
The dispersal is in part due to the success prosecutors have had in depleting the Camorra in recent years, Bobbio added.

While a small wing of the Camorra is still involved in national and international drug-trafficking, the Neapolitan mob draws much of its strength by preying on the local economy through contraband sales and extortion on businesses.

In Sanita, one of Naples' most populous and crime-ridden districts, people shrug off the latest outbreak of mob violence. The attacks of the last months have prompted national outrage only because mobsters have begun hitting middle and upper-class neighbourhoods, they say.
"Here, it's a daily event. People live in terror," says Roberto Colonna, 78, a barber in the heart of the district.
Sanita has been in the grip of organised crime since the early 1980s when the mob took control of a major building boom.

"Ten years ago, there were three clans here. Then some members were killed and it was quiet for a while. In the last year, another two have sprung up and the shootings have started again," Colonna says.
FEAR AND SILENCE TRIUMPH
Besides inter-gang violence, shopkeepers are often prey to mobster loan-sharking, adds Colonna, a union leader in the area.
"Even at rates of 150 percent, if you don't pay, you risk shutting down. The threats start with gunshots at your windows and gasoline thrown on your door and it goes on," he says.
The Camorra, residents say, is something everyone knows exists but no one dares talk about.
"When a man I had been warned about came in and asked for free medicine, I gave it -- no questions asked," said Carla De Lellis, 35, a pharmacist in Sanita.
Throughout the city, all crime, even the rampant pick-pocketing for which Naples is famous, is tied in some way to the mob.
"Youths here start by stealing a tyre, then a moped. Gradually they become known," Colonna said.

Residents say the root of widespread organised crime in the region is high unemployment. While Naples has seen a revival in the last three years, it is still one of Europe's poorest cities with unemployment at close to 25 percent.
Naples mayor Antonio Bassolino and several prosecutors criticise Italy's infamously slow justice system.
This week, 30 alleged Camorra members on trial for gunning down an 11-year-old boy during a clan fight were released from jail because court procedures were taking too long.
The judge said he had set them free because the trial -- which after five years is still at its initial stages -- was lasting longer than the legal limit on preventive custody.
"This shows the schizophrenia of the justice system. On the one hand we send in the army and on the other we let 30 bosses go," says a senior police source, declining to be named.
Even for small-time crimes, police estimate that that, out of 40 crooks they catch, only one or two stay in jail.
"We need to look carefully at the working of the justice machine. It is slow, while many people arrested for events linked to organised crime return too soon to freedom," Bassolino said.
OFFICIALS SAY TROOPS CAN'T CRACK THE CAMORRA
Italy's Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano said this week that some 500 to 600 soldiers would be sent to Naples during the next three months.
The troops are supposed to take over routine guard duties around the city, allowing hundreds of police officers to be redeployed to fight organised crime.
But Naples police and prosecutors agree the army is not a solution to the city's Camorra problem.
"Having the army here will help safeguard Naples' image. But I don't think it will help in our battle against the mob. Much more is needed to break the network," Bobbio says.
Residents, however, will be pleased to see the troops.

"The military should have come ages ago. At least it will bring some tranquility," says Patrizia, a 35-year-old mother in the middle-class Vomero area where last month a woman was killed by a stray bullet as she was walking home with her young son.
"All districts are risky now. I fear for my children and for myself," says Patrizia, who asked not to be further identified.
Prosecutors hope the attention which recent attacks have prompted will help residents and the national government realise the force of the Camorra in Naples.
"The (Sicilian) Mafia has always gotten more attention in national politics. But the Camorra has never stopped being a menace," Bobbio said. "It constitutes a national emergency."
